articles.title: ‘The butcher may be gone, but to many he is a hero’: victims condemn glorification of Mladić
articles.description:
Architect of Srebrenica genocide is dead but those scarred by his atrocities say his ideology is still shockingly pervasive

To most of the world, he was and will always be the “Butcher of Bosnia”, a grim epithet but one that still fails to fully convey the evil and horror inflicted on its people by Gen Ratko Mladić, who died in prison on Thursday.

As commander of the Bosnian Serb forces, Mladić was responsible for the killing of an estimated 100,000 men, women and children during the savage breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s. He was most notoriously the architect of ethnic cleansing and the genocide at Srebrenica in which at least 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were slaughtered.

articles.title: Artist defends Ronnie O’Sullivan mural in Sheffield saying it isn’t finished
articles.description:
Critics say painting looks more like a zombie but artist Chris Ashmore says ‘touch-ups’ are still to happen

A street artist has defended his mural of the snooker player Ronnie O’Sullivan in Sheffield after critics suggested the world champion looked like a zombie.

Chris Ashmore was commissioned to produce the artwork featuring the former seven-time world champion for the back wall of the Spot On snooker club, the BBC reported.

articles.title: ‘Confluence of errors’ led to Belgian tourist Celine Cremer’s death in Tasmanian wilderness, coroner finds
articles.description:
Coroner finds 31-year-old deviated from a walking track as dusk fell, four days before the winter solstice

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Overlapping errors, including a lack of preparation in near-freezing winter weather, contributed to the death of a Belgian tourist on a wilderness track.

Celine Cremer set off on a walk at Philosopher Falls in Tasmania’s remote north-west on 17 June 2023 and was reported missing almost 10 days later.

articles.title: Flight attendant’s breast cancer was occupational disease, court rules
articles.description:
Sophie Lainault, who worked for Air France, wins legal case linking illness to more than 12,600 hours on flights

A flight attendant in France has succeeded in having her breast cancer recognised as an occupational disease, a first for the country’s aviation industry, her lawyer and a trade union said.

The ruling, which recognised that Sophie Lainault, a former flight attendant for Air France, had frequently worked at night and been exposed to passive smoking, could pave the way for similar claims, the lawyer and the CFDT union said.

articles.title: Raygun opens up on her infamous Olympics breakdancing debut: ‘not as bad as I thought!’
articles.description:
Australia’s first Olympic breakdancer became a viral sensation after her performance at Paris 2024, where she failed to receive a single point

Rachael “Raygun” Gunn says her performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics was “not as bad as I thought!” after the Sydney-based breaker revealed she had finally watched back the moment that catapulted her to international fame – and mockery.

The Sydney academic turned speaker was Australia’s first Olympic breakdancer and became a viral sensation after her unconventional routine at Paris 2024, where she failed to receive a single point from the judges.

articles.title: Andrew Tate rented supercars to appear ‘uberwealthy’, says his lawyer
articles.description:
Self-described misogynist and his brother, Tristan, are playing role to generate income from online attention, Miami court filing says

Andrew Tate rented supercars and borrowed a yacht to appear “uberwealthy” and generate online engagement, his lawyer has said.

Legal representatives for the self-described misogynist social media influencer and his brother, Tristan Tate, have claimed the pair deliberately portray themselves as far wealthier than they are because their “business model depends on online attention”.

articles.title: Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds
articles.description:
Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running

The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.

Experts have said this demonstrates the “serious threat” datacentres pose to the UK’s legally binding climate goals.

articles.title: Yorkshireman believed to be first Briton to die fighting for Russia against Ukraine
articles.description:
Bradley Townsend reportedly killed by a drone on 10 June in Donetsk region after joining up with separatists

  • Europe live – latest updates

A man from South Yorkshire is believed to be the first British citizen to die fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.

Bradley Townsend, a 33-year-old fisher from Barnsley, left Britain in April to join up with Russian separatists in eastern Donbas to aid in their invasion of Ukraine, despite having no previous combat experience or familiar ties to eastern Europe. Alongside 49-year-old Ben Stimson and 39-year-old Aiden Minnis, Townsend was granted Russian citizenship for joining the country’s military campaign.
